local_facts.claim: California Civil Code section 3342 makes a dog's owner liable for a bite suffered in a public place, or anywhere the bitten person was lawfully present including the owner's own property, regardless of the dog's former viciousness or the owner's knowledge of it. Code of Civil Procedure section 335.1 gives an injured person two years from the date of the bite to sue.
local_facts.why_it_matters: States on the common law one-bite rule require proof that the owner already knew the animal was dangerous. California does not, so an owner saying the dog has never bitten anyone is not a defense. The two-year limit is the real pressure: it runs from the bite itself, it is not extended because an insurer is still negotiating, and a claim against a public agency's dog has to be presented within six months instead.
local_facts.title: California does not make you prove an earlier bite

local_facts.claim: San Diego County Code section 62.615 requires anyone who knows of a bite by a rabies-capable animal to notify the Department or Health Officer. That includes the bitten person, the parent or guardian of a bitten child, the treating physician and the animal's owner. A failure to report within 24 hours is a violation. County Animal Services says a biting dog must then be quarantined for ten days from the date of the bite even if its rabies vaccination is current.
local_facts.why_it_matters: The report and the quarantine file are third-party documents that fix the date, the address and the identity of the dog before anyone's memory changes. They are often the strongest evidence in a claim the insurer did not create, and they also reveal whether this dog has bitten before. Which agency holds the file depends on the address: San Diego Humane Society handles field services for the City of San Diego, County Animal Services covers the unincorporated areas.
local_facts.title: A San Diego bite is reportable within 24 hours

local_facts.claim: The 2023-2024 San Diego County Grand Jury dog bite report found that roughly 2,500 dog bites a year were reported by the county to the California Department of Public Health over the 2020 to 2022 period. About 40 percent involved dogs that were unvaccinated or of unknown vaccination status, and the true figure is higher because not every city files its statistics. It also recorded 9 to 18 Dangerous Dog hearings a year, of which 78 to 90 percent ended in a dangerous declaration.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Reported bites in this county run into the thousands every year, so an owner's claim that the incident was freakish carries little weight. The vaccination gap explains why so many San Diego bite victims face a rabies prophylaxis decision in the emergency room, which is a real cost item. And because a large share of Dangerous Dog hearings succeed, that county process can produce findings about the animal that sit alongside a civil claim.
local_facts.title: About 2,500 bites a year are reported here

fee_rows.stage: The share taken from a bite recovery
fee_rows.note: No California statute limits the percentage in a dog bite matter. Rule 1.5(a) bars an unconscionable or illegal fee and stops there.

fee_rows.stage: The only percentages California does fix
fee_rows.note: Section 6146(a) limits fees to 25 percent, or 33 percent once a complaint is filed, in professional negligence claims against health care providers.

fee_rows.stage: The contract handed over at signing
fee_rows.note: Section 6147(a) requires a written contract signed by attorney and client, with a duplicate copy given to the client that same day.

fee_rows.stage: The sentence about negotiating the rate
fee_rows.note: Under 6147(a)(4) a claim outside section 6146 needs a contract stating the fee is not set by law and can be negotiated.
